video_title: Is the CFTC's Kalshi Rescue a Dangerous Precedent? - DEX in the City
gist: Three crypto lawyers (host Jesse, plus guests Jane and Jacob of the Law of Code podcast) argue that the CFTC's use of its Section 8a(9) emergency authority to keep Kalshi trading despite state litigation is legally defensible for prediction markets but sets a precedent that could be turned against any industry, and that the fight is headed to the Supreme Court. They also dissect the SEC's abruptly cancelled ~400-page crypto rulemaking (and the fading odds of the CLARITY Act), Anthropic's worldwide Claude watermarking as an example of EU AI Act extraterritoriality, and a new presidential memorandum letting vetted private firms run offensive cyber operations under DOJ/DHS supervision.

themes.theme: CFTC emergency authority vs. states' rights

insights.claim: The CFTC invoked Section 8a(9), its emergency authority, to direct Kalshi to keep operating under CEA core principles and 'maintain orderly trading' regardless of ongoing state litigation — an authority that by the host's research has been used only about six times in history, with two of those uses coming in the past month and both for Kalshi.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest, Law of Code podcast host) and Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: A statutory tool reserved for systemic market catastrophes is now being deployed as a shield for a single venue's business model — watch whether other CFTC registrants start seeking the same protection from state enforcement.
insights.quote: the CFTC invokes section 8A9 which is its emergency authority to direct a registered exchange in this case Kali to take steps to what they call maintain orderly trading

insights.claim: The host argues the real risk is normalization: once an unelected agency can declare an 'emergency' to override state court proceedings on a sympathetic issue like prediction markets, the same mechanism becomes available on abortion-pill interstate shipment, gun rights, or any other contested issue under a future administration.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: Regulatory wins won via emergency powers are fragile and reversible; investors underwriting prediction-market exposure on the basis of CFTC protection are betting on a precedent that cuts both ways.
insights.quote: the choosing of what is an emergency based on what that agency thinks is important at that time gives me a little bit of concern

insights.claim: The host flags a direct ideological inconsistency in crypto: the industry campaigned hard to have Chevron deference overturned on the grounds that unelected agencies should not hold sweeping authority, and is now cheering an agency's use of emergency action authority.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: Signals that the crypto lobby's administrative-law arguments are outcome-driven, which weakens their durability in court and should temper confidence in agency-granted protections.
insights.quote: all of crypto fought for you know Chevron to be overturned not all of it but a big chunk of it right because agencies shouldn't have so much authority if they're not elected right that was a lot of the argument and now we're saying let's give the agencies emergency action authority

insights.claim: The counter-argument is structural: because the state suits against CFTC-registered exchanges in New York, Minnesota and elsewhere are all substantively identical, the CFTC either has to intervene in every one or in none, which makes selective non-intervention untenable and the emergency order close to forced.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: Expect the CFTC to keep issuing parallel orders rather than pick winners — a repeatable pattern that de-risks federally registered venues until a court says otherwise.
insights.quote: if you intervene in one case, you have to intervene in them all because they're all very, very similar cases when it comes to going after these CFTC regulated exchanges

insights.claim: All three panelists converge on the prediction that the federal-versus-state jurisdictional question over prediction markets ends at the Supreme Court, with the operative issue being whether Congress actually granted the CFTC the authority it is now asserting.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest) and Jane (guest)
insights.so_what: A binary, multi-year legal overhang sits over every prediction-market venue and its equity/token holders; position sizing should reflect an eventual all-or-nothing ruling.
insights.quote: ultimately I think this is why it's going to go to the Supreme Court because the question is does the CFTC have the authority that they are saying they have from a congressional perspective

themes.theme: Prediction markets vs. gambling: product distinction

insights.claim: Jacob's framework distinguishes prediction markets from gambling houses by back-end mechanics rather than user interface — 'the button looks the same,' but the settlement and market structure differ the way equities markets differ from derivatives markets.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: The winning legal and product argument for prediction markets is infrastructural, not cosmetic — venues that can document exchange-like mechanics are better positioned than those that lean on betting UX.
insights.quote: they are fundamentally different products even though the button looks the same you're betting on outcome but how it works on the back end really is what separates different types of exchanges

insights.claim: After a three-hour podcast interviewing both pro- and anti-prediction-market voices, Jacob reports that every single participant — including opponents — agreed prediction markets and regulated gambling should both be able to exist, with prediction markets skewing institutional and gambling houses serving retail seeking rewards.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: Coexistence rather than displacement is the base case — the institutional hedging segment, not retail sports betting share, is where prediction-market TAM should be modeled.
insights.quote: every one of them said both should be able to exist. and they thought that prediction markets might be more for institutions in the future whereas gambling houses could be more for people who want things like rewards

insights.claim: The most persuasive real-world use case cited is a California goat-herding business that used Kalshi via Castle Labs to hedge the risk that a tax break for goat herding would not be extended — an actual commercial hedge that covered in Matt Levine's Bloomberg column, CNBC and elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: Concrete commercial-hedging use cases are the strongest defense against the 'it's just gambling' framing — track how many non-sports, real-hedge contracts venues can point to as a legal-risk indicator.
insights.quote: an actual person that runs a goat hering business. They needed to hedge the fact that like this tax break for goat hering would not potentially extend indefinitely

insights.claim: Jacob reframes the harm question by asking who is actually being protected: he suggests the injured parties in state actions may be tribes, gaming commissions and existing license holders defending a moat, rather than the residents the consumer-protection rationale invokes.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: Frames the state litigation as incumbent rent defense — useful for handicapping which states fight hardest (those with the largest licensed gaming economies).
insights.quote: Is it actually residents of New York or is it the tribes, the the gaming commissions, the people who currently have some form of power?

themes.theme: SEC rulemaking vacuum and CLARITY Act odds

insights.claim: The SEC abruptly cancelled a proposed crypto rulemaking that was reportedly around 400 pages and would have delivered comprehensive market-structure rules or guidance in the absence of the CLARITY Act passing, citing a scheduling conflict that the panel believes was pretextual.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: The near-term path to US crypto market-structure clarity just narrowed to legislation only — a materially worse setup for projects that were sequencing launches against expected SEC guidance.
insights.quote: It was canceled. It was very vague. There was a scheduling conflict that was cited, which is probably not really the case.

insights.claim: Two competing explanations circulate for the cancellation: White House actors not wanting SEC rules to relieve pressure on the CLARITY Act, or traditional securities-industry incumbents resisting rules that would enable tokenization of securities.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: If the incumbent-resistance explanation is right, tokenized-securities infrastructure faces a slower regulatory runway than the current institutional-adoption narrative implies.

insights.claim: The host assesses that the odds of the CLARITY Act passing are 'plummeting by the moment,' and Jane separately says she is not optimistic — meaning the panel expects neither the legislation nor the cancelled SEC rules to deliver clarity in the near term.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host) and Jane (guest)
insights.so_what: Plan for continued US regulatory ambiguity through the cycle; sub-regulatory guidance, not statute, is the realistic best case for builders and institutional entrants.
insights.quote: the odds of that are plummeting by the moment. I haven't fully given up hope.

themes.theme: EU AI Act extraterritoriality and Claude watermarking

insights.claim: Anthropic rolled out statistical watermarking for Claude worldwide rather than by region, explicitly because of the EU AI Act's August content-marking requirement — another instance of the EU exporting its rules to every user globally because the product cannot be split by jurisdiction.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: Confirms the Brussels-effect pattern for AI: compliance costs and product changes driven by EU law land on US users and should be modeled into every frontier-lab product roadmap.
insights.quote: everyone in the world, just like we've seen before, gets the EU rule. Uh, Brussels is making this decision and we all Chicago is getting it as well.

insights.claim: The watermarking mechanism is not hidden characters or labels but token-selection bias: when the model picks between two equally good next words, the choice is now driven by a secret key rather than a coin flip, letting Anthropic statistically prove Claude authorship after the fact.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: Provenance detection is probabilistic and key-dependent, so third-party verification requires the decoder — a structural limit on how useful watermarking can be for scam and fraud detection.
insights.quote: every time the model picks between two equally good words sort of to anticipate what the next word should be, the choice is now based on a secret key instead of the coin flip concept

insights.claim: Jacob raises a First Amendment compelled-speech argument against AI watermarking: if a US user drafts an email with Claude, the model's forced output modification alters the user's speech to a counterparty without the user knowing what changed or how to remove it.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: A viable constitutional attack vector on EU-driven AI mandates in US courts — a live litigation catalyst for AI policy that few are pricing.
insights.quote: there's an argument that it's a form of compelled speech where now anthropic is changing is forced to change its output

insights.claim: Jane's framing of the EU AI Act — 'a hammer when you need a scaffold' — is that overregulation will push companies out of the EU without stopping bad actors, mirroring what she believes happened with MiCA and EU privacy rules.
insights.speaker: Jane (guest)
insights.so_what: Continued capital and company flight from the EU in both AI and crypto is the expected second-order effect — relevant for jurisdiction-selection in venture and token launches.
insights.quote: I think it's a hammer when you need a scaffold. And it's the same way I felt about Mika.

insights.claim: Jacob's structural critique is that EU regulation systematically punishes compliant actors, using cookie consent as the proof case: the rule failed to stop tracking, degraded the user experience, and put companies that voluntarily declined to track at a competitive disadvantage — and AI watermarking will repeat the pattern since anyone wanting to disclose AI use already would.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: Compliance-driven mandates create adverse selection against good actors — a reusable lens for pricing regulatory risk in both AI and crypto compliance products.
insights.quote: So, you're actually punishing the good guys.

insights.claim: Watermarking is already technically compromised and over-inclusive: decoders exist on GitHub, the scheme requires the model provider to opt in so bad actors can simply route around it, and a single AI-edited word in an otherwise human document can trigger the mark.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: AI-provenance detection should not be underwritten as a durable moat or a working anti-fraud control — the tooling defeats it faster than regulation deploys it.
insights.quote: there's already decoders on GitHub for it. Unclear if they're fully going to work, plus you have to have the model buy into it. And so are the bad actors really going to use this?

themes.theme: CFTC as first mover on AI in markets

insights.claim: The CFTC is holding the first meeting of its Innovation Advisory Committee this Thursday, covering crypto, prediction markets and AI in markets — making it the first US regulator to publicly examine how autonomous systems should operate in markets.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: An under-the-radar agenda-setting event: the CFTC's framing of agentic trading liability will likely become the de facto US baseline before any legislation exists.
insights.quote: the CFTC is being the first US regulator sort of sit down and examine in a more public sense like how to regulate AI in markets

insights.claim: The open questions on agentic systems in markets — mens rea, liability, accountability — remain entirely unresolved, and the host characterizes the current state of building autonomous market systems as 'a bit of yolo.'
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: Firms deploying autonomous trading agents are carrying unquantified legal risk; early CFTC guidance is the first real pricing input for that exposure.
insights.quote: including men's rhea liability accountability, but hopefully we get a little bit of clarity back to that word there on how people should be building these systems because right now it's a bit of yolo

themes.theme: Cyber letters of marque: private offensive operations

insights.claim: The US president signed a memorandum on approximately August 12 expanding capabilities against transnational organized crime in cyber, establishing a program under DOJ and DHS supervision that lets vetted private companies run offensive cyber operations, building on a March executive order and a national coordination center created in 2025, with implementation criteria due within 60 days.
insights.speaker: Jane (guest)
insights.so_what: A concrete 60-day window creates a near-term commercial opening for cybersecurity and blockchain-forensics firms that can qualify as government agents.
insights.quote: issued a memorandum related to like expanding capabilities in combating transnational um transnational organized crime focused specifically on cyber

insights.claim: Jane pushes back on the prevailing 'vigilante justice' reading of the memorandum: participating companies become agents of the government, must comply with domestic and international law, and need DOJ or DHS permission once agreements are in place — with annual assessments of adherence to procedures.
insights.speaker: Jane (guest)
insights.so_what: The program is far more constrained than headlines suggest; expect slower response times and heavy compliance overhead, not a free-for-all hacking market.
insights.quote: these private companies are going to have to understand that they, you know, if there are cases that are brought, right, if there's an investigation, they're now an agent of the government

insights.claim: The host draws a historical analogy to privateering — a system that ended not on principle but because governments could not control the privateers — and warns that the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act was not repealed, so participants still operate against a live criminal statute whose bounds the government may lack the technical expertise to police.
insights.speaker: Jesse (host)
insights.so_what: Legal exposure for participating firms is not eliminated by the memorandum — diligence on any vendor claiming offensive-cyber authorization should test the specific written government mandate.
insights.quote: it's also like reminds me a lot of the privateeering part of our history which didn't shut down for any reason but that they couldn't control the privateeers out on the water

insights.claim: Jacob uses the Drift hack — roughly $280 million, much of it in USDC, with public pressure on Circle to freeze funds — to argue the speed problem is real: Circle takes on major private and government liability risk when it acts without a court order or government mandate.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: A formal government mandate mechanism would materially change stablecoin issuers' freeze behavior in hacks — a structural improvement in recovery odds worth tracking for anyone holding stablecoin-denominated risk.
insights.quote: when Drift was hacked, there was I think it was like $280 million and and much of it was in USDC and people were clamoring for Circle to freeze it

insights.claim: Jacob frames the memorandum as 'cyber letters of marque' and analogizes the expected outcome to what SpaceX and commercial entrants did for aerospace — a large gain in efficiency and talent from opening a government monopoly to private operators, conditional on implementation details.
insights.speaker: Jacob (guest)
insights.so_what: If the analogy holds, a new private cyber-defense contracting category is forming — early-stage opportunity for blockchain-analytics and offensive-security firms positioned to qualify.
insights.quote: directionally giving out some cyber letters of mark so that we can have people who go out on especially on blockchains but just in the digital space
